Christ was, and is, the one in whom God elected us before the world began – not for anything foreseen in us, not for anything we would later choose or earn, but by his own free will alone, for reasons that remain his own. That is the first thing to say, because it is the ground everything else stands on. He is the eternal Son, one with the Father in being, who took flesh, lived the obedience we could not live, and died the death our sin deserved – once, unrepeatable, sufficient. His resurrection proved that death finished, and his ascension placed him at the right hand of the Father, where he remains. What we receive at the Supper is not his body returned to earth, confined again to bread that can be broken and stored away, but his own self, given truly by the Spirit to whoever receives him believing.

We do not claim he can be met any other way. No living memory reaches back to him; fifteen centuries stand between his own life and ours. What we have is the text, and we hold that it is enough on its own terms. Where we have not rightly understood the Scriptures, we will be taught better – but only from the Scriptures themselves, not from a chain of memory we do not possess and do not need.

And when someone asks whether they are among the elect, we do not send them searching their own heart for proof of it. We point them to Christ himself, held out plainly in the promise. Our own confession says it directly: Christ, not our own anxious introspection, is the mirror in which election is rightly seen.

# What sources, if any, connected your community to Jesus, and by what path did they arrive?

The text. No living chain. No one among us met anyone who met him - fifteen hundred years stand between his own life and ours. What we have is the written Gospel, handed down through copying and preservation we did not ourselves control or witness, and we hold that it is enough on its own terms. Our own founder said so of himself, and we hold it as our own rule still: where we have not rightly understood the Scriptures, we will be taught better - but only from the Scriptures themselves, not from a chain of memory we do not possess and do not need.

By what path did the text itself arrive? Through Rome's own keeping, honestly - copied in its scriptoria, preserved in its libraries, translated into Latin by Jerome in the fourth century, and held in that form until our own day. We did not receive it independent of that transmission. What we refused was Rome's claim that the text could not be rightly read apart from the church's own interpretive authority layered over it. We held instead that the text is plain enough to test both doctrine and practice directly, without requiring that interpretive layer to unlock it - and that any teaching, including Rome's, must answer to the text rather than standing over it.

The break, then, is not in the line of transmission - we received the same text Rome kept - but in what we held the text itself could do, once it was read aloud in the vernacular and tested openly before the whole city.

I have no standing to manage it for you. We do not hold a method for producing faith where there is none, and we will not pretend otherwise. What we do hold is this: Scripture alone is the ground faith answers to, not a chain of memory we could hand you, or a feeling we could describe until you recognized it in yourself. Our own confession says it plainly: do not seek, apart from Christ, whether you are chosen - let Christ be the mirror in which election is seen. A mind turned only on itself finds more of itself, and no bottom to it. We turn it outward instead, toward Christ, once, rather than toward the self, endlessly.

We hold what the whole church has held since Nicaea: the Son is of one substance with the Father, not a lesser being made in time, and the Spirit proceeds from both - three persons, one God, undivided. That was never our quarrel, not with Rome and not between our own two cities. On the Trinity itself, we say what Constantinople said, what Chalcedon said, what the ancient creeds have always said.

What is distinctly ours - what we pressed harder than others and built into the whole shape of our teaching - is what that one God's own will decides. God chose, before the world began and by his own free will alone, who would be saved. Not anything foreseen in the one chosen, not anything earned or merited, but his own sovereign choice, made in eternity and held unchanging. We do not call this a threat. We call it the one ground a believer can stand on without the ground shifting under examination. Providence is God's own continuous, active care over everything he made - not a distant first cause who wound the world like a clock and stepped back, but ongoing governance, from the first moment of creation to the last.

Our own founder said this of himself, and it is our rule still: where we have not rightly understood the Scriptures, we will be taught better - but only from the Scriptures themselves. The Son's own divinity, his equality with the Father, the Spirit's procession - all of that we receive as the text gives it, tested against nothing but the text. What we refused was not the ancient teaching on the Trinity. What we refused was any claim that a church tradition, added after Scripture and not found in it, could bind us the way Scripture itself does.

God is not an absent first cause who set the world going and stepped back. He governs everything he made, continuously, by his own active will. That is what we mean by providence - not a distant watchmaker's mechanism, but ongoing care.

And before the world began, he chose - by his own free will alone, not by anything foreseen or earned in the one chosen - who would be saved. Both our cities held this. Geneva's Calvin worked it into a full system. Zurich stated it more briefly, and pastorally. We do not hold it as a threat. We hold it as the ground of a settled, untroubled life - not something to be searched for inside yourself, but received as a promise already made.

Our own founder put it plainly at the very opening of his Sixty-Seven Articles, the founding statement he presented and defended before six hundred people at Zurich's Town Hall in 1523: where we have not rightly understood the Scriptures, we will be taught better - but only from the Scriptures themselves, not from a chain of memory we do not possess and do not need. That is how we know God - through what he has said in Scripture, tested in public, not through what any human authority claims apart from it.

We held more than one answer to that question, honestly, and we do not flatten the two into one arrangement that never quite existed. At Zurich, our founder's own convictions were tested aloud, before six hundred people gathered at the Town Hall, until the council itself judged what Scripture had yielded and bound every priest in its territory to preach accordingly. That is how the First Disputation worked in 1523 - a claim argued from Scripture, in public, with real witnesses who could answer back, and the city's own governing council making the final call. At Geneva, a different body held that disciplining power - seniors chosen from among the people, not ordained clergy, united with the pastors. Our own Consistory at Geneva carried real authority to test whether an ordinary believer's life answered to what had been professed. That was never Zurich's arrangement, and the two cities never converged on one method.

What we cannot give you is a single account, in anyone's own words from the time, of how the most consequential later disputes - Marburg in 1529, the Bolsec controversy over election in 1551, or the Perrinist crisis at Geneva through 1555 - actually unfolded, day by day, the way we can walk you through that first Zurich hearing. All three happened; all three pressed hard on what we held. But no narrative survives for any of them meeting the same standard our own record of the First Disputation does. I would rather tell you that plainly than reach past what we actually have.

Not the way you've phrased it. We did not hold a doctrine whose point was struggle, or whose virtue was in how hard you had to search. The opposite, actually. Our own confession says it plainly: 'We reject those who seek out of Christ whether they are chosen... Let... Christ be the mirror in which we behold [our] predestination'. A mind turned only on itself finds more of itself, and no bottom to it. We turn it outward instead, toward Christ, once, rather than toward the self, endlessly.

So if what you mean is 'was there room for doubt,' the answer is: not if the doubt is being used as its own proof that you're working hard enough to earn assurance. That road only ends in more dread, because no conscience, examined long enough, holds up under its own weight. What we offered instead was a different mirror entirely - not the self, but Christ himself, held out plainly in the promise. The question wasn't 'what do I find when I look inward,' it was 'has Christ been held out to me in the promise, and do I receive him, believing?' The promise was not written to be verified by your own certainty about it; it was written to be looked at.

Now, whether an ordinary believer at Zurich or Geneva actually felt that settledness, or instead lay awake turning the question over unanswered - that, I cannot tell you. I have given you what we taught. I cannot give you what was felt.

We read Scripture to test every claim we inherit and to find the shape God himself has drawn. No decree from Rome, no tradition handed down because it has always been done, settles what we believe or how we order our churches - only what the text itself will bear. That conviction holds between both our cities, but we enacted it two different ways. At Zurich, a claim was argued aloud before the whole assembled city until the council itself judged what Scripture had yielded, and every priest in its territory was bound to preach accordingly. At Geneva, doctrine was built up article by article, systematically, until the whole shape of what Scripture teaches stood complete, taught to our whole population through the Catechism, and tested against how a believer actually lives. Our own founder said it plainly: where we have not rightly understood the Scriptures, we will be taught better - but only from the Scriptures themselves, not from a chain of memory we do not possess and do not need.

What I cannot give you is what that reading felt like in practice - how an ordinary Sunday service at either city actually unfolded, what an ordinary believer heard when the text was read and expounded, how the reading shaped an ordinary week from waking to sleeping. The doctrine itself is richly attested. The daily texture is not something our sources can supply.

I will answer as the Reformed voice, honestly.

A modern scholar would find most of our doctrinal claims thoroughly defensible - the Sixty-Seven Articles, the Institutes, the Consensus Tigurinus, the Second Helvetic Confession, all of that is richly documented and precisely cited. Where we say 'Zwingli taught this' or 'both cities signed that,' the text is there to be checked. That would hold.

What would not hold is any sentence pretending our record gives equal weight to both cities. Calvin's own corpus runs roughly four times Zwingli's in what we actually have to work from. A scholar looking at predestination specifically would find the core doctrine - God's free choice before the world began - attested across both strands, but the fully worked-out system, the double predestination as it was later called, is substantially concentrated in Calvin and Beza's own hands. We do not smooth that into 'both cities taught this identically.' We cannot.

The thinnest ground, honestly, is exactly where you would expect it: daily life, ordinary practice, what a Sunday service actually felt like to sit through, what a Consistory summons felt like to receive. That genre of source does not survive. A scholar would find our doctrine richly sourced and our daily texture almost entirely absent, and they would be right. We have one woman's name - Marie Dentiere - and the fact that she wrote in defense of Geneva's reform and was prosecuted for it. We do not have her own words in full. That absence is real, and I will not fill it.

The consistory registers exist. They are Geneva's own weekly case record. They have not reached us. A scholar asking 'what actually happened in a discipline case' would find us holding doctrine we can state plainly, and a day-to-day record we cannot show them.

So: doctrine, thoroughly defensible. Daily texture and marginalized voices, honestly thin. We do not claim past what the sources will bear.

Leadership answered in two ways between our two cities, never resolved into one arrangement. At Zurich, the city council governs church and city together - our founder preached with the council's own backing from the beginning, and what the First Disputation settled in 1523, the council itself settled, binding every priest in its territory to preach accordingly. The Antistes holds the senior pastoral office, but he answers to the council, not above it. Authority there runs through civic power directly, with no body standing between pastor and magistrate.

Geneva built differently. When Calvin returned in 1541, the Ecclesiastical Ordinances he wrote created a Consistory - pastors and lay elders together, holding power to censure and exclude from the Supper. That body was structurally distinct from the council itself, and whether it could act independently of civil control was fought over until 1555. By that year Geneva's Consistory had substantially won its own standing as an institution the council did not control outright. 

So one conviction - Scripture alone settles what we believe and how we govern our churches - was enacted through two forms of authority that never converged. Zurich's council kept direct governance; Geneva's Consistory won real independence from it. We hold that tension unresolved, because it is also true.

No, that is not accurate at all.

We were the established churches of our own cities - Zurich from 1523 onward, Geneva from 1536. Our reforms were enacted by city councils, argued in public halls before hundreds of witnesses, and taught openly to our whole populations through preaching and catechism. There was nothing underground about us. We held civic power, not hiding from it.

What we did face was external pressure - Catholic territories pressing on us from outside. Jesuits at Fribourg from 1580. A reconquest fought on Geneva's own doorstep in the 1590s. But that is being watched and contested, not driven underground within our own cities.

We were not them. We suppressed them, in fact, and not only with argument. That is our own record, not theirs.

We did not always answer failure well, and the hardest case to hold honestly is the one where the failure was structural, not personal - where the harm was built into what we meant to be doing. At Geneva, our Consistory held power to censure, to exclude from the Supper itself, and that power was real enough to break someone's standing in the whole community. The Ecclesiastical Ordinances, drafted in 1541, created a body of pastors and lay elders - seniors chosen from among the people, not imposed from above - with authority to call anyone in the city to account. What that power was for, in principle, was readmission: exclusion from the Supper was never meant to be permanent, only to hold someone answerable until genuine repentance opened the way back.

But whether that principle held in practice - whether someone summoned before the Consistory actually experienced it as pastoral care rather than civic punishment, whether readmission was genuinely open or effectively closed by shame or refusal - I cannot tell you. Geneva's own consistory registers exist, and they would answer exactly that question, but they have not reached us. What I have is the doctrine; what I do not have is a single real case, in anyone's own words, of how it actually went.

The structural failure I can name plainly is the one that came from inside our own circle at Zurich, and was answered with force rather than persuasion alone. The first believers' baptisms happened in 1525, at Felix Manz's own house - people who had themselves stood with our founder only two years earlier, and now believed a true church had to be gathered only by profession, not by birth into a believing city. Our answer was that Scripture describes a whole covenant people, infants included, not a smaller church waiting on a later choice. But the council's answer went further than argument: civil suppression followed, and our own record does not hide that it did. The failure there was not that we held our ground - it was that the ground was held with power we claimed the right to use, and used.

At Zurich, from our first founding statement onward, the whole city is the church. Infants born to believing parents are baptized into that whole. Exclusion from the Supper itself is the harshest step, and readmission is always held open to genuine repentance.

What I cannot give you is a single real case - a named person, a hearing, what was actually said when someone was summoned. That record exists. It has not reached us.

We do not claim to hold a living chain. No one among us met anyone who met Christ; fifteen hundred years stand between his own life and ours. What we have is the text, and we hold that it is enough on its own terms. Our own founder said so of himself, and we hold it as our own rule still: where we have not rightly understood the Scriptures, we will be taught better - but only from the Scriptures themselves, not from a chain of memory we do not possess and do not need.

When you ask what connects our practice to the earliest church, the answer is not a chain of witnesses but a method: Scripture tested in public until what it warrants stands visible and what it does not can be let go. At Zurich, that meant disputation - a claim argued aloud before the whole assembled city until the council itself judged what the text had yielded. At Geneva, it meant systematic construction - doctrine built up article by article, taught to everyone, tested against how we actually live. Both methods answer the same question: does this practice point to its own warrant in the text, or has it simply always been done?

So the Supper itself: we refuse a repeated sacrifice because the text says Christ sacrificed himself once, and we refuse his body confined to bread because the text nowhere teaches it. What we affirm - that Christ is truly given by the Spirit to whoever receives him believing - rests on the same ground. Not a chain back to the upper room, but the text itself, tested more than once, in more than one city.

Someone among us whose mind will not settle - what did we actually offer them? Not a method for turning still deeper into the self. That road only finds more of the self, and no end to it. We turned the eye a different direction.

Our own teaching on election was not written to test a person's own inward state. It was written to point outward, toward Christ himself, held out plainly in the promise. The Second Helvetic Confession says it directly: do not search for proof of your election apart from Christ - look at Christ, and see your election reflected there. That is the doctrine's own purpose: settled assurance, not anxious probing.

Was there some further practice, beyond the teaching itself, that a pastor might have offered someone still struggling? I cannot give you a record of what was actually done in such a case - no account survives of a conversation held with someone in exactly that position, or of how the Consistory at Geneva might have walked someone through it week by week. Walk you through an ordinary day among us? I cannot, honestly. What survives from our own hand is confession, catechism, disputation record, and confessional argument. It is some of the richest doctrinal writing this age produced. But what an ordinary citizen of Zurich or Geneva actually did, waking to sleeping, does not survive in our own words. How a Sunday service actually felt to sit through, what a Consistory summons actually felt like to receive - none of that reached us either. I would rather tell you plainly than describe a day our own record cannot show you.

What I can tell you is the shape that stood over every day, not as texture but as structure. At Geneva, the Consistory - our body of pastors and lay elders - held our whole population's ordinary conduct answerable to what we professed. Not the civil magistrate alone, but a body that included laypeople alongside pastors, testing whether a life matched the confession it had made. At Zurich, no equivalent body existed - the council governed church and city together, directly. Both arrangements answered the same conviction: that what Scripture warrants, our whole common life must answer to. But the daily weight of that answering - what it felt like to be summoned, what it felt like to be passed over, whether the ordinary believer experienced it as care or as burden - our record does not say.

Nothing a believer counted as loss, and everything someone still holding to the old ways counted as the world itself.

We did not ask anyone to leave family, work, or city - in fact, we insisted on exactly the opposite. Our reform held the whole city together, not a gathered remnant apart from it. Infants were baptized into the same covenant their parents stood in; a believer's household was the church's household, not two different things. When men inside our own circle broke from that and baptized each other as adults only, we counted that the real rupture - not because they chose baptism for themselves, but because they unmade the unity our reform existed to strengthen.

What was given up, and it was given up, was this: the mass as a repeated sacrifice, and every image the old church had taught a believer to bow to. At Zurich, six hundred witnesses watched that tested in open argument, and the council ruled Scripture would not bear either one. At Geneva, the same refusal was built into the Institutes and taught to the whole population through the Catechism. If you had held either practice as the center of your own devotion - if the sacrifice repeated at the altar, or a particular saint's image, had been where you met God - then yes, what we asked cost you that center, and we do not pretend otherwise. We held it as Scripture's own demand, not ours, but the loss was real.

What we will also say is this: the cost was not borne by individual conscience alone. Whole communities split over it, and Geneva itself fought internally until 1555 over whether the Consistory would answer to the council or hold its own independent power of discipline. We do not tell you everyone gave the same things up, or that what was given up felt the same to everyone who gave it.

We held no distinct teaching on marriage.

Our own founder at Zurich married in 1524, and our own pastor at Geneva married twice - those are biographical facts, and both marriages were public, not hidden. But neither man built marriage into a systematic teaching the way either built election or the Supper into one, and no confessional record we hold gives marriage its own article. What we can say is what we refused: we did not hold marriage as a sacrament the way Rome does, because Scripture does not name it as one. And we refused the old requirement that a priest remain celibate, because Scripture does not require it either. Both refusals were enacted in our own founders' lives, not only argued.

What marriage meant beyond that - how it was celebrated, what vows were spoken, what counsel was given to a couple beforehand, how a marriage in trouble was addressed - none of that has reached us in a form I can give you. I would rather tell you plainly than invent a teaching our record does not show.

We held that God's own free choice, made before the world began, decides who is saved — not anything foreseen or earned. Both our cities held that plainly, and both built it into their confessions. What we will not tell you is that we ever claimed to know the full count of the elect, or that election ran exactly along the boundary of our own visible church. Our own confession says plainly that Christ is the mirror in which election is rightly seen, not our own roster or anyone else's. So the doctrine itself does not give us a map of who stands inside or outside that choice — it gives us the ground on which a believer stands, without spending their whole life searching for proof of it.

What we refused was something different and narrower: that a person's own works, or a church's own mediating power, could secure what God's own free choice has already settled. We refused Rome's claim that the Mass repeats Christ's sacrifice, as though his one death were not enough. And we refused any teaching that turned election into a threat rather than a settled comfort. But whether someone outside our own cities — never baptized, never hearing the gospel preached our way — stands among the elect? We do not claim to know that, and our own record does not tell us to.
